Venetian harbor and Koules fortress

Fortress · 40 min

The sea fortress built by Venice to guard Crete.

WHAT'S HERE, IN WALKING ORDER
Arrival 8:00 am
Stand here: On the harbor breakwater, facing the fortress at the entrance of the old port.
This is the Koules, the Venetians' Castello a Mare, the Fort on the Sea. It guards the entrance to the old port of Heraklion, and the Republic of Venice built it in the early 16th century. Mind your footing out here. If waves are breaking over the breakwater, don't go out along it. Stay by the fortress. Venice bought its claim to this city in 1204 and called it Candia. To hold it, over the centuries that followed, the Venetians built a giant wall with seven bastions, and a fortress in the harbor. This one. There may have been a fort here since Arab times, and later there was a Byzantine tower. The Venetians knocked it down in 1523. To make the platform bigger, they filled old ships with stone and sank them as a breakwater. The fortress was finished in 1540.
▶ Play
The fortress 8:10 am
Stand here: At the fortress entrance, looking at the thickness of the walls.
The fortress comes in two parts: a tall rectangular block and a lower, rounded section. In places, the walls are 8.7 meters thick. Inside, on two floors, there were 26 rooms: barracks, a prison, storerooms, a water reservoir, a church, a mill and a bakery. A small town, sealed in stone. In 1630 it carried 18 cannons on the ground floor, and 25 more along the way up to the roof. If you get up to the parapet, look out to sea toward the islet of Dia. Jacques Cousteau found many sunken remains of Cretan sea trade out there. On the northern part of the fort is a lighthouse tower; a lighthouse was built here under Egyptian rule, between 1830 and 1840.
▶ Play
The siege of Candia 8:20 am
Stand here: On the breakwater, looking back toward the city.
This fort's great test was the siege of Candia. The Ottomans besieged the city from 1648 to 1669. That's 21 years, one of the longest sieges in history. The fort didn't count for much in the siege. Ottoman guns easily put its firepower out of action. In the end, on 27 September 1669, the Venetian commander, Francesco Morosini, with only 3,600 fit men left, accepted terms and surrendered. The cost was terrible. By one account, in the final 22 months alone, some 70,000 Turks, 38,000 Cretans and slaves, and 29,088 of the city's Christian defenders died. Under the terms, all Christians could leave Candia with whatever they could carry. And Morosini? He'd surrendered without the Venetian Senate's permission, and for years he was a controversial figure back home. One more strange detail from the Venetian archives: a plan to break the siege by infecting the Ottoman soldiers with plague. It was never carried out.
▶ Play
Closing 8:30 am
Stand here: If the sea is calm, walk a little way out along the breakwater and look back; if not, stay where you are and look back at the fortress.
The Ottomans changed little here, adding some battlements. They built a small fort on the land side, Little Koules, but it was torn down in 1936, when the city was being modernized. Today the fortress is restored and open to visitors. The breakwater runs on for almost 1.2 mi, with views back over the city and the ferry port. Look at the fort against the city. For 21 years, it was part of a defense that people would not give up. Take a moment before you walk back.

Venetian harbor and Koules fortress

Fortress · 40 min

The sea fortress built by Venice to guard Crete.

WHAT'S HERE, IN WALKING ORDER
Arrival 8:00 am
Stand here: On the harbor breakwater, facing the fortress at the entrance of the old port.
This is the Koules, the Venetians' Castello a Mare, the Fort on the Sea. It guards the entrance to the old port of Heraklion, and the Republic of Venice built it in the early 16th century. Mind your footing out here. If waves are breaking over the breakwater, don't go out along it. Stay by the fortress. Venice bought its claim to this city in 1204 and called it Candia. To hold it, over the centuries that followed, the Venetians built a giant wall with seven bastions, and a fortress in the harbor. This one. There may have been a fort here since Arab times, and later there was a Byzantine tower. The Venetians knocked it down in 1523. To make the platform bigger, they filled old ships with stone and sank them as a breakwater. The fortress was finished in 1540.
▶ Play
The fortress 8:10 am
Stand here: At the fortress entrance, looking at the thickness of the walls.
The fortress comes in two parts: a tall rectangular block and a lower, rounded section. In places, the walls are 8.7 meters thick. Inside, on two floors, there were 26 rooms: barracks, a prison, storerooms, a water reservoir, a church, a mill and a bakery. A small town, sealed in stone. In 1630 it carried 18 cannons on the ground floor, and 25 more along the way up to the roof. If you get up to the parapet, look out to sea toward the islet of Dia. Jacques Cousteau found many sunken remains of Cretan sea trade out there. On the northern part of the fort is a lighthouse tower; a lighthouse was built here under Egyptian rule, between 1830 and 1840.
▶ Play
The siege of Candia 8:20 am
Stand here: On the breakwater, looking back toward the city.
This fort's great test was the siege of Candia. The Ottomans besieged the city from 1648 to 1669. That's 21 years, one of the longest sieges in history. The fort didn't count for much in the siege. Ottoman guns easily put its firepower out of action. In the end, on 27 September 1669, the Venetian commander, Francesco Morosini, with only 3,600 fit men left, accepted terms and surrendered. The cost was terrible. By one account, in the final 22 months alone, some 70,000 Turks, 38,000 Cretans and slaves, and 29,088 of the city's Christian defenders died. Under the terms, all Christians could leave Candia with whatever they could carry. And Morosini? He'd surrendered without the Venetian Senate's permission, and for years he was a controversial figure back home. One more strange detail from the Venetian archives: a plan to break the siege by infecting the Ottoman soldiers with plague. It was never carried out.
▶ Play
Closing 8:30 am
Stand here: If the sea is calm, walk a little way out along the breakwater and look back; if not, stay where you are and look back at the fortress.
The Ottomans changed little here, adding some battlements. They built a small fort on the land side, Little Koules, but it was torn down in 1936, when the city was being modernized. Today the fortress is restored and open to visitors. The breakwater runs on for almost 1.2 mi, with views back over the city and the ferry port. Look at the fort against the city. For 21 years, it was part of a defense that people would not give up. Take a moment before you walk back.
